$comment: The black-and-gold colour system, and the single upstream every stella-facing
surface generates from. Normative definition: SPEC-stella-tui-v2.md sections 2-4.
Do not hand-edit a generated artifact. Edit this file, run `make tokens-update`,
and commit the regenerated files alongside it. `make tokens` fails the gate when
a generated file has drifted from this one, which is the mechanism replacing the
prose promise that four surfaces had been copying by hand.
Every token declares a `clamp` role. The role decides which predicate the value
is held to, so a new hex cannot enter the palette without a human choosing the
kind of colour it is -- and the warm-drift predicates reject the choice that
kills a gold-on-black scheme. The predicates are defined once in
crates/stella-tui-theme/src/clamp.rs and mirrored by scripts/check-tokens.py;
both are held to this file's `clamps` block below.
Every token also declares a `paint` posture, for the same reason and against a
different failure. `clamp` asks what KIND of colour this is; `paint` asks
WHETHER ANYTHING RENDERS IT. Nothing asked that until #4975, and `comment`
is what got through: a published token with a role sentence, a --st-comment
declaration on four surfaces, a COMMENT constant in the generated token.rs,
a row in the SPEC's palette table, three design renderings using its hex, a
row in the contrast ratchet -- and no call site anywhere. One of the sub-AA
pairings #4063 was deciding about was a colour no reader had ever seen. This
is AGENTS.md invariant #10 (`every emitted signal names its consumer`) pointed
at the palette, and crates/stella-protocol/src/event/consumers.rs is the shape
it copies: a declared posture per row, enforced from both sides.
Two postures, and the guard checks each against the tree rather than trusting
it -- a declaration nothing verifies is what `comment`'s `role` field already
was:
"paint": "painted"          some hand-written surface names this token,
as var(--st-<css>) or as token::<rust>. The
sweep fails if it finds none.
"paint": { "gap": "#N" }   nothing names it, and #N is where that is being
decided. The sweep fails if it finds a site --
a gap that has been closed must be redeclared,
not left standing.
What the sweep can and cannot see is stated at check 4 in
scripts/check-tokens.py. The short version: it is a NAME sweep, not a render
trace, so it cannot follow a value copied under another name. Eleven of the
web stops below sat at `gap` for exactly that reason -- the site shipped
their values as literals under --stella-* rather than through var(--st-*).
#4978 completed the two hand-mirrored sheets and repointed those roles, so
they are `painted` now: the fix the posture asked for, rather than a posture
written to match the code.
name: oxagen house system

reason: The house kit changed on 2026-11-02 (oxageninc/brand, branch true-gold-cool-palette),
and this file follows it so the two brands stay one palette. The grounds are now
cool: soot #090A0D on the dark side and bone #FCFCFE on the light side, with blue-grey
between them. The zinc ramp leaned violet, near OKLCH hue 286. The new greys sit near
The gold is still #D4AF37. On a light ground the gold is always darker than on a dark
one, so the lift on dark is now #E3C45B and the gold ink on light is now #806719.
Two choices differ from the kit. Stella keeps its panel and raised surfaces on bone,
because a lift of one percent cannot be seen in a terminal, so they share the paper hex
where the kit paints them white. And Stella keeps one grey, #6E727A, for hints on soot
and for secondary text on bone, where the kit holds two. It clears 3:1 on soot and 4.5:1
on bone. The neutral clamp did not move.

why: The green ratio is the hue clause: below it the hue is orange, and orange on
a near-black ground reads brown on cheap panels. It moved from 78 to 70 with
the house gold, and the account of that is plain: 78 was never measured. It
was the ratio v5.0's own gold happened to sit at, written down as a law.
#D6962C is at 0.701 and is unmistakably gold, so 78 excluded golds rather
than oranges.
70 is a floor with an argument behind it: sRGB hue 30 deg is the orange the
clause exists to exclude, and a colour at r > g > b with g = 0.70 r sits at
or above sRGB hue 36 deg, six degrees clear of it. Anything below 0.70
crosses into that band.
The ratio carries one role. `gold-ink` is a dark SHADE of the gold, which a
hue ratio polices badly because darkening moves a colour's channel ratios;
the shade is anchored instead. See `gold-shade`.

gold-lift.predicate: r > g > b AND 100*g >= 70*r AND hue within 4 deg of `anchor` AND lighter than `anchor`
why: A lift is anchored to the gold it lifts, never held to a second blue
ceiling. A revision of this file carried `lifted-gold` with blue_pct 44 -- a
bound reverse-engineered from the one token it had to admit, which can say
no to nothing in principle. It was answering the wrong question: in a
gold, lightness is (r + b) / 510, so the resting ceiling 100*b <= 35*r
caps lightness for ANY colour, and a lift sits above that line. There the
ceiling is not strict, it is unsatisfiable.
So the two clauses are stated where each is coherent. The green ratio is
the HUE rule -- gold versus orange -- and it holds at every lightness, so
every gold carries it. The blue ceiling is the SATURATION rule and governs
only the resting gold, which is not lightened. A lift is then pinned to
the anchor: same hue within hue_tolerance_deg, strictly lighter.
An anchor is the stronger constraint, not the looser one. A ceiling admits
every colour beneath it and keeps passing after the gold it was cut for is
gone; an anchor admits only the authored gold, brighter. Recolour `gold`
and leave `gold-bright` behind and the check fails, naming the hue
distance.
hue_tolerance_deg is derived, not chosen: stella-tui's v1 theme records
that its warning amber sat 4.0 deg from gold 'so an outcome may never be
told from chrome by hue alone'. 4 deg is the distance this repository
already treats as indistinguishable, so a lift -- which must be the SAME
hue -- sits inside it. It was written as 3 while the only lift on file
happened to sit at 2.9; the house pair sits at 3.0, which is what exposed
the number as a measurement of one sample rather than a law.

gold-shade.predicate: r > g > b AND hue within 4 deg of `anchor` AND darker than `anchor`
why: The mirror of `gold-lift`. `gold-ink` is the gold where the metal itself is
illegible: as text or a hairline on paper, where #D6962C is 2.2:1. Same hue,
darkened.
A ratio is the wrong tool for it. Darkening squeezes a colour's channels
unevenly, so a shade's g/r drifts from its parent's for reasons that are not
about hue. Hold a shade to a ratio and the ratio has to drop until it lets
the shade in. A ratio that wide stops holding the hue of the bright one.
An anchor asks the question that counts: is this the SAME gold, darker?
Recolour `gold` and `gold-ink` fails by name. A ratio cannot do that.
Green, amber and red are deliberately neither metal nor neutral. SPEC 2
asks for them desaturated and cool; that is a review judgement, not a
channel predicate, so no predicate is asserted rather than a decorative
one being invented. What DOES hold them is the 30 deg hue-separation law,
enforced by scripts/check-hue-separation.py over every pair of chromatic
roles in both schemes -- which is the check that made v6.0 move the
warning when the identity moved toward it.

surface.why: Diff row backgrounds are tints carrying a sign column, not hues in a role. They are held by the diff renderer's contract (the + and - signs are mandatory), not by a channel test.

why: One neutral clamp for the whole system, ink to paper. The house system's
blue-grey ramp leans a few units blue (its muted-ink stop spreads 14).
A black-and-gold scheme must not let a grey carry a hue: a tan grey competes
with the gold, a blue one fights it. A bound on the spread of the channels
says exactly that, in both directions. 12 is the loosest bound that still
rejects a sepia grey spreading 13, and every stop of the cool ramp clears it
except the kit's two secondary greys on paper, which take the nearest value inside it.

$comment: Web-only stops. Every token below carries no `rust` name, because the
terminal never draws it and every entry in the generated `ALL` table
needs a 256-colour fallback -- an ANSI approximation of a paper tint
would be an assertion about nothing. `scripts/gen-tokens.py` skips
them, so `crates/stella-tui-theme/src/generated.rs` is unchanged.
They are declared here rather than left in the site's stylesheet
because that is what puts them under a clamp. Until now the only file
that knew the site's warning hue was the site, and the 30-degree
separation law that governs it on the terminal was, on the web, a
sentence in a comment (#4071). The light ramp is the one #4072 records
as derived rather than specified; specifying it here is what closes
that gap.
The values themselves are unchanged -- these are the stops the site
already ships, moved under the system rather than re-cut.

$comment: Hexes that may not appear anywhere outside this file and the generated
artifacts that carry the supersession note. Each entry names where it came
from, so a reader hitting the guard learns which retired system they are
looking at rather than only that they are wrong.
Most entries are the anchors of a superseded kit. Five are not, and they
arrived by two different routes.
Four were never a kit at all. website/public/presentations/investor-deck.html
carried its own warm palette, matching neither v1.0 nor v2.0, and it shipped
on a public URL beside two other brand generations (#3653). A value nobody
specified has exactly the same standing here as one that was retired --
no legitimate use -- so it is banned on the same list rather than a
second one. The tree carries none of the four; they are listed so
reintroducing one fails, which is what #3653's own Verify step asks for
and what nothing did until this entry existed.
The fifth is `comment`, a v5.1 token of THIS kit that nothing ever painted
(#4946). It is banned rather than merely deleted because deleting it leaves
the value sitting in three design renderings and two brand tables, where the
next reader reads it as live.
